# Benchmarking & Profiling {#profiling} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-2_11db5e50107dde7eb9832b44b304d7c5'} ::: **Benchmarking** is the process of timing the execution of code for the purpose of comparison. For example, you can compare the execution time of a program in two different systems, e.g. a laptop and a high performance server. Another common case is to compare the performance of two different programs that produce the same output on the same computer. **Profiling** refers to timing the different steps of a program to identify bottlenecks and potential targets for optimization. ## `system.time()`: Time the execution of an expression The base package's `system.time()` function allows you to measure the execution time of an R expression. ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-3_193ae175409ce87445e32286d4fced73'} ```{.r .cell-code} system.time(rnorm(9999999)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` user system elapsed 0.305 0.007 0.312 ``` ::: ::: "elapsed" time is real time in seconds. "user" and "system" are time used by the CPU on different types of tasks (see `?proc.time`). As always, you can pass any R expression within curly brackets: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-4_48661d56982758d89f46feac5875e895'} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- rnorm(9999) system.time({ for (i in 2:9999) { x[i] x[i] <- x[i]^3 } }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` user system elapsed 0.002 0.000 0.002 ``` ::: ::: You can use `replicate()` to get a measure of time over multiple executions and average it: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-5_2e88d24214ec4dce0d65efcf1aa37380'} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2020) x <- matrix(rnorm(500000), nrow = 5000) y <- 12 + x[, 3] + x[, 5]^2 + x[, 7]^3 + rnorm(5000) fit.glm <- function(x, y) glm.fit(x, y) fit.glm_time10 <- replicate(10, system.time(fit.glm(x, y))[[1]]) ``` ::: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-6_c203384bdf8fe456763bc4eabe246d97'} ```{.r .cell-code} boxplot(fit.glm_time10) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Profiling_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=240} ::: ::: ## Compare execution times with `microbenchmark::microbenchmark()` The [**microbenchmark**](https://github.com/joshuaulrich/microbenchmark/) package's `microbenchmark()` function allows you to time the execution of multiple expressions with sub-millisecond accuracy. It will execute each command a number of times as defined by the `times` argument (default = 100), and output statistics of execution time per expression in nanoseconds. Using `plot()` on the output produces a boxplot comparing the time distributions. ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-7_01b0227578f5494efe1ba0dc812eb8d0'} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("microbenchmark") library(microbenchmark) ``` ::: ### Example: loop over matrix vs. data.frame Let's create `xmat`, a 500 by 5 matrix and, `xdf` a data.frame with the same data. ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-8_927249f0f957c9f53af7ff7224639748'} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2021) xmat <- matrix(rnorm(500 * 5), nrow = 5) xdf <- as.data.frame(xmat) ``` ::: If you wanted to square either of them, you would just use `^2`. Here, we create a function specifically to demonstrate the difference in working on a numeric matrix vs. a data.frame by using a nested loop that replaces each element one at a time. ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-9_c92f4c2677c2b398d336a8aa68124ffe'} ```{.r .cell-code} silly_square <- function(x) { for (i in seq_len(NROW(x))) { for (j in seq_len(NCOL(x))) { x[i, j] <- x[i, j]^2 } } } ``` ::: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-10_db32ff0123849fee22108fc77c3b270a'} ```{.r .cell-code} mat_df_sq <- microbenchmark( silly_square_mat = silly_square(xmat), silly_square_df = silly_square(xdf), mat_squared = xmat^2, df_squared = xdf^2 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in microbenchmark(silly_square_mat = silly_square(xmat), silly_square_df = silly_square(xdf), : less accurate nanosecond times to avoid potential integer overflows ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(mat_df_sq) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "microbenchmark" "data.frame" ``` ::: ::: Print microbenchmark's output: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-11_651ee67b405d34d97bcb0d830fca5c12'} ```{.r .cell-code} mat_df_sq ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Unit: microseconds expr min lq mean median uq silly_square_mat 107.543 111.7865 135.07614 114.431 117.6905 silly_square_df 40335.472 42334.3655 43649.35645 43320.272 44353.2875 mat_squared 1.107 1.8655 3.05122 2.911 3.6900 df_squared 9875.793 10685.0305 11735.24427 12122.388 12624.4945 max neval 2190.753 100 71158.042 100 15.990 100 16040.963 100 ``` ::: ::: Notice how a) either operation is much faster on a matrix vs. a data.frame and b) vectorized squaring with `^2` is much faster than the nested loop as expected. There is a `plot()` method for microbenchmark objects: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-12_5c92f2e56255979e6e0cfd167d5cece3'} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(mat_df_sq) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Profiling_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ### Example: Group means Let's perform a simple mean-by-group operation and compare three different approaches. As an example, we use the `flights` dataset from the **nycflights13** package which includes data on 336,776 flights that departed from NY area airports in 2013. The data comes as a [tibble](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/), and we create data.frame and data.table versions.th ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-13_e8252aad0274db6216cc0ca2e419a0d8'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(nycflights13) library(data.table) options(datatable.print.class = TRUE) class(flights) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} dim(flights) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 336776 19 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} flights_df <- as.data.frame(flights) flights_dt <- as.data.table(flights) ``` ::: Compare performance of the same operation using different functions: * base R `aggregate()` with formula input * base R `aggregate()` with list input * base R `tapply()` ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-14_ddbffe9b5e95346dd90acde80ade0ee5'} ```{.r .cell-code} flights_aggregate_formula <- function() { aggregate(arr_delay ~ carrier, data = flights_df, mean, na.rm = TRUE) } flights_aggregate <- function() { aggregate(flights_df$arr_delay, by = list(flights_df$carrier), mean, na.rm = TRUE) } flights_tapply <- function() { tapply(flights_df$arr_delay, flights_df$carrier, mean, na.rm = TRUE) } groupmean_3x <- microbenchmark( aggregate_formula = flights_aggregate_formula(), aggregate = flights_aggregate(), tapply = flights_tapply() ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-15_7df570fa0a0af5578ead66e1f09c705f'} ```{.r .cell-code} groupmean_3x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Unit: milliseconds expr min lq mean median uq max neval aggregate_formula 49.984125 56.19456 59.13615 57.88038 60.38195 97.78959 100 aggregate 43.398500 46.89822 49.91139 48.52676 50.61108 86.17450 100 tapply 9.478421 10.48790 11.85747 10.71896 11.61592 50.03513 100 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-16_a5cd1d8ab6c8e560e25408b1787992d5'} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(groupmean_3x) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Profiling_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ## Profile a function with `profvis()` The **profvis** package's `profvis()` function provides an interactive output to visualize the time spent in different calls within a program. ::: {.cell hash='Profiling_cache/html/unnamed-chunk-17_bed7c3b87404a6a77c8d5815244cc444'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(profvis) profvis({ hf <- read.csv("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/00519/heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv") str(hf) lt5 <- which(sapply(hf, \(i) length(unique(i))) < 5) for (i in lt5) hf[, i] <- factor(hf[, i]) index_numeric <- which(sapply(hf, is.numeric)) par(mfrow = c(1, length(index_numeric))) for (i in index_numeric) boxplot(hf[, i]) par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) }) ``` :::
